Applications.data: The Hall-Effect Thruster is commonly used to maintain satellite orbits because of its fuel efficiency (high specific impulse).
As of August 2019, over 150 Hall-effect Thrusters have been successfully launched and operated by Maxar, the company building the Psyche Orbiter.
They have also been utilized for materials processing such as ion implantation and ion etching for semiconductor manufacturing.
Currently there is research into using these thrusters for deep space probe applications with the Psyche Mission being the first to use a Hall-effect Thruster beyond lunar orbit.

PsycheUse.data: The Hall Thruster will be used on this mission for an interplanetary cruise from Earth to Psyche.
When at Psyche, it will perform transfers between the science orbits at the asteroid.
Transfers between the different orbits A to B and B to C require about 3 weeks of thrusting with the final change from Orbit C to D requiring 4.5 months of thrusting.

Background.credit: NASA Chris Lynch NASA ID: GRC-2015-C-01191

Background.data: Hall-effect Thrusters were studied both in the United States and Soviet Union in the early 1960s with the first successful propulsion device coming out of the Soviet Union.
The first SPT to operate in space, an SPT-50 aboard a Soviet Meteor spacecraft, was launched December 1971.
The first use of Hall thrusters on lunar orbit was the European Space Agency lunar mission SMART-1 in 2003.
The first flight of an American Hall thruster on an operational mission was the Busek BHT-200, which launched December 2006 on a Department of Defense Space Test Program mission called TACSAT-2.

FunFacts.data: The Psyche Mission will be the first mission to use Hall thrusters beyond lunar orbit.
The trade-off for the achievable high exhaust speeds is the low thrust or acceleration. So it can take a very long time for it is reach its final destination.
Since Hall thrusters use inert gas for propellant, there are no risks of reactivity with anything else in its feed system as there are with chemical rockets.
Hall thrusters are able to accelerate their exhaust to speeds anywhere between 5 and 50 miles per second.
Hall thrusters operate on a variety of propellants, the most common being xenon and krypton. Other propellants of interest include argon, bismuth, iodine, magnesium and zinc.
